centralThesis: Stranded clean electricity at remote mega-sites such as the ~60 GW / ~300 TWh-per-year Yarlung Tsangpo project should be exported not as electrons over lossy ultra-long-distance transmission, nor wasted as curtailment, but as AI inference (tokens) over fiber, because compute embeds energy at roughly 10 to 1,000 times the value density of either electrons or 20th-century "canned electricity" such as aluminum.
novelty: Prior framings treat stranded clean power as a transmission problem (build more UHVDC) or AI's energy use as a sustainability liability (data centers as a growing load to be decarbonized). We invert both: we recast the data center as an energy-export terminal and the token as the highest-value-density carrier yet found for stranded electricity, extending the century-old "congealed electricity" logic of siting aluminum smelters at remote hydro (Iceland, Norway, Pacific Northwest, Quebec) into the information age. Timeliness is sharp and multi-pronged: (1) the Yarlung Tsangpo project broke ground July 2025 with no published power-evacuation plan and Tibet's local demand (~12-13 TWh) is ~4% of its output; (2) west-China curtailment spiked in H1 2025 (Tibet wind 30.2%, solar 33.9%); (3) frontier inference energy intensity is now credibly bottom-up quantified (~0.3-4 J/token, Epoch AI 2025 / Joule 2026); and (4) global token throughput just crossed ~10^16/yr and is growing several-fold annually (Google 3.2 quadrillion tokens/month, May 2026). For the first time the electricity-per-token, the stranded resource, and the global demand are all large and measured enough to compare directly, which no prior Perspective has done quantitatively.
workedExample:
YARLUNG TSANGPO / MEDOG WORKED EXAMPLE (60 GW, 300 TWh/yr, COD ~2033).

Step 0 — Site. 60 GW installed, 300 TWh/yr (3x Three Gorges), CF 57%. Busbar LCOE C_src = $0.040/kWh central (range $0.030 China-low to $0.057 global-avg/remote). Tibet local demand only ~12-13 TWh/yr, so >95% of output must leave the plateau; nearest eastern load centers are >2,000 km away. H1 2025 Tibet curtailment already 30-34%, so the counterfactual to a buyer is partly *waste*, not sale.

Step 1 — Electron export (Path A). Over ~2,500 km UHVDC: losses ~8% central; levelized adder ~$0.020/kWh at design utilization, but realistically ~$0.036/kWh at ~56% utilization (the historical norm for new west-China lines feeding a variable-but-here-firm source). Delivered cost ~$0.063/kWh; the exported product is a commodity kWh worth ~$0.05-0.08 at destination. Net exportable value density: ~$0.05-0.08 per source kWh. Transmission capex for ~60 GW of evacuation: multiple +/-800-1,100 kV corridors at ~$0.6/W => order $36B+ of dedicated lines, stranded if under-utilized.

Step 2 — Token export (Path B). Co-locate compute; export over fiber (energy cost of fiber transport is negligible). Useful tokens/kWh T at central epsilon=2.2 J/tok => 1.64M tokens/kWh. Electricity contributes c_elec = $0.024 per million tokens. Sold even at the cheapest 2026 budget price (~$0.40/Mtok), gross value is ~$0.66 per source kWh; at mid-tier ($15/Mtok), ~$25/kWh; at frontier ($75/Mtok), ~$123/kWh. Even net of the ~93-95% of revenue that pays for chips/facility/labor, residual value per kWh dwarfs the $0.05-0.08 of electron export.

Step 3 — Total output and global share (SENSITIVITY TO epsilon, the dominant uncertainty).
- epsilon = 0.7 J/tok (best-case batched): 1.5e18 tokens/yr => ~30-86x global throughput.
- epsilon = 2.2 J/tok (Epoch central): 4.9e17 tokens/yr => ~10-27x global throughput.
- epsilon = 4 J/tok (Joule median): 2.7e17 tokens/yr => ~5-15x global throughput.
- epsilon = 40 J/tok (frontier/reasoning, pessimistic): 2.7e16 tokens/yr => ~0.5-1.5x global throughput.
HONEST HEADLINE: "At today's efficiencies this single site could produce on the order of the entire world's current annual token throughput, and plausibly several times it; under reasoning-heavy, large-model workloads that fall to ~once-over global demand." The claim survives even the pessimistic corner.

Step 4 — The binding constraint (where the example breaks the naive reading). 60 GW of compute = ~40 million H100-class GPUs and ~$2.3 trillion of capex — ~14x the $167B dam itself, and a multiple of current annual global AI-accelerator output. So the site cannot be filled at once; it is a 10-20 year compute build-out, chip-supply-limited, not energy-limited. The correct reading is directional: the *marginal* economics overwhelmingly favor exporting tokens, but realized scale is gated by hardware, capital, and chip geopolitics, not by the physics of the watt.

ASSUMPTIONS/RANGES TO STATE: C_src optimism (remote mega-dam may exceed $0.04); epsilon spans ~100x and dominates every downstream number; global-throughput denominator is itself uncertain (~2-3x) and growing several-fold/yr; market token prices are falling ~80%/yr; transmission adder is utilization-sensitive. Present every headline as a range, never a point.
comparisonTable:
| Export carrier for 1 kWh of stranded clean energy | What physically leaves the site | Energy lost / overhead to "package" it | Transport medium & its loss | Gross product value per source kWh | Value-density vs raw electron | Key constraint |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Electrons (UHVDC)** | The kWh itself | Converter + line losses 6-10% over 2,000-3,000 km | +/-800-1,100 kV line; ~3-3.5%/1,000 km | ~$0.05-0.08 (delivered wholesale) | 1x (baseline) | Fixed line capex; utilization 21-56% doubles per-kWh cost; needs demand at the other end |
| **Aluminum (Hall-Heroult)** | ~69 g of metal (14.5 kWh/kg) | Electrolysis is the use; ~40% of metal cost is power | Ship/rail metal; ~0 energy loss in transit | ~$0.14-0.20 (LME ~$2,600/t) | ~3x | Alumina/anode/labor inputs; metal price cycles; smelter collapses if power stops being cheap (PNW 1979-2001) |
| **AI tokens (inference)** | ~1.6 million tokens (at 2.2 J/tok) | Datacenter overhead in PUE (folded into J/tok); electricity only ~4-7% of TCO | Fiber; ~0 energy loss, latency ~tens of ms/1,000 km | ~$0.7 (budget $0.40/Mtok) to ~$25 (mid $15/Mtok) to ~$123 (frontier $75/Mtok) | ~10-1,000x | Hardware/chip capex dominates (~60% of TCO); chip supply & geopolitics; latency-sensitive workloads can't relocate |

outline.heading: Title: Export the watt as a token
outline.content: Claim-forward title (<=12 words). Standfirst/teaser: stranded clean power should leave remote mega-sites as AI inference over fiber, not as electrons over wire. Signals genre = thesis-driven Perspective, not review.

outline.heading: Abstract (~180 words, unstructured, no refs)
outline.content: 4-move arc: (1) Stakes — the world is building ~60 GW / 300 TWh-per-yr hydro (Yarlung Tsangpo) far from any demand, while west-China curtailment hit 30%+ in 2025; the default answer is thousands of km of lossy UHVDC. (2) Claim — we argue the highest-value way to export stranded clean energy is to convert it on-site into AI tokens and ship those over fiber. (3) Case — electricity is only ~4-7% of compute cost and ~0.024 $/million tokens; a token embeds energy at 10-1,000x the value density of an electron or of aluminum, the 20th-century 'canned electricity'; at measured inference efficiencies this one site could produce on the order of, to several times, the entire world's current annual token throughput. (4) Implication — treat premier stranded-energy sites as compute terminals; the binding limit becomes chips and capital, not transmission.

outline.heading: Introduction (no subheads)
outline.content: Four-move ladder. Background+anchor: the Yarlung Tsangpo project (approved Dec 2024, broke ground Jul 2025, ~$167B, 5 cascade stations, ~2033) will generate ~300 TWh/yr — ~72% of all 2024 global data-center electricity — in a seismically active gorge >2,000 km from demand, with Tibet consuming only ~12-13 TWh. Conventional framing: an evacuation problem solved by UHVDC under West-East Power Transmission. Why now: convergence of (i) groundbreaking with no published evacuation plan, (ii) 2025 curtailment spike (Tibet wind 30.2%/solar 33.9%), (iii) bottom-up inference energy now measured (~0.3-4 J/token), (iv) global throughput crossing ~10^16 tokens/yr growing several-fold annually. Claim stated explicitly ('Here we argue...'). Roadmap paragraph naming the five moves.

outline.heading: §1 The stranded-power problem and why moving electrons is the wrong default
outline.content: Sub-claim: long-distance electron export is lossy, capex-heavy, demand-dependent, and chronically under-utilized. Marshal: UHVDC losses 6-10% over 2,000-3,000 km; converter stations ~1/3 of cost; the decisive point — line capex is fixed so per-kWh cost scales inversely with utilization, and China's early UHV lines ran 21-56%. Only ~20% of UHV throughput is renewable. Quantify delivered cost $0.053-0.074/kWh and note the product sold is just a commodity kWh. Bridge: there is a precedent for exporting energy as a higher-value good instead.

outline.heading: §2 Tokens as 21st-century canned electricity (the reframing + historical analogue)
outline.content: Sub-claim: civilizations have always monetized stranded power by embedding it in a transportable product; tokens are the densest such product yet. Analogue: aluminum as 'congealed electricity' — 13-16 kWh/kg, ~40% of cost is power, smelters deliberately sited at stranded hydro (Iceland ~64-72% of national electricity to smelters; Norway; Quebec; Kemano/Kitimat; PNW Bonneville). Crucial cautionary half of the analogue: the PNW model collapsed when power stopped being cheap (rates +250%, all 10 smelters idled by 2001) — co-located energy-export industries live and die by cheap power, exactly the comparative advantage a stranded mega-hydro confers. Reframe the data center as an energy-export terminal. Bridge: quantify the value density that makes tokens different.

outline.heading: §3 Why the token wins: the quantitative core
outline.content: Sub-claim: per source kWh, tokens are worth 10-1,000x electrons or aluminum, and electricity is a trivial share of token cost. Present the framework: tokens/kWh from epsilon (0.7-70 J/token); electricity contributes only $0.006-0.44 per million tokens vs $0.40-180/Mtok market price; electricity ~4-7% of TCO (hardware ~60%). The value-density ladder figure (electrons $0.05-0.08; aluminum $0.18; tokens $1-123). Worked Yarlung Tsangpo example with full sensitivity to epsilon: ~2.7e16 to 1.5e18 tokens/yr => ~0.5x to ~30x global throughput. State the headline as a range and flag epsilon as the dominant uncertainty. This is the evidential heart; the key figure lives here.

outline.heading: §4 Feasibility: what would have to be true
outline.content: Sub-claim: the model is physically and operationally plausible for the right (latency-insensitive, batchable) workloads. Enabling conditions: cold/high-altitude free-cooling (Google Hamina PUE 1.09) suits the Tibetan plateau; fiber adds negligible energy and only tens of ms latency per 1,000 km, fine for batch inference, training, agentic/reasoning jobs, synthetic-data generation; precedent of computing as flexible/location-agnostic load (Bitcoin mining as 'buyer of last resort' for curtailed/flared energy — Crusoe >250 MW, ERCOT flexible load, Texas-wind mining studies). Honest gaps: water/cooling at altitude, seismicity (M8.5 design near a suture zone), chip logistics into one of Earth's most inaccessible regions. Bridge: but the deepest objections are economic and geopolitical.

outline.heading: §5 Counterarguments, limits, and risks (dedicated section)
outline.content: Engage strongest objections in best form, concede then bound. (1) Hardware, not energy, dominates — TRUE; ~$2.3T capex / ~40M GPUs for 60 GW means the constraint is chips/capital/time, so the claim is marginal-economic and multi-decade, not a switch to flip. (2) Why not build the data center near demand? — because the comparative advantage is the cheap stranded watt and avoided transmission; near-demand siting forgoes both and competes for congested grids. (3) Latency-sensitive workloads can't relocate — concede; only the batchable fraction qualifies (but it is large and growing with reasoning/agentic jobs). (4) Firm hydro has high grid value — opportunity cost is real where a grid exists; here local demand is ~4% of output and curtailment is 30%+, so grid value is largely notional. (5) Water/cooling, seismicity, altitude. (6) Jevons/rebound — cheap tokens may expand demand, not cut energy. (7) Geopolitics of compute — concentrating frontier compute at one state-controlled trans-boundary-river site raises export-control, sovereignty, and downstream-water (Brahmaputra) concerns; the same logic applies to stranded renewables in democracies (ERCOT, Chile, Quebec, Nordics). Do not rebut to zero; show the claim survives within a bounded envelope.

outline.heading: Conclusion / Outlook (no subheads)
outline.content: Restate significance: the watt's best export route is increasingly the token; premier stranded-energy resources should be planned as compute terminals alongside, or instead of, transmission. Concrete, falsifiable next steps naming actors: (i) grid planners/IRENA should publish a delivered-value-per-kWh metric comparing electron vs token vs metal export per site; (ii) operators should pilot a GW-scale curtailment-financed inference cluster at a curtailed renewable site (Texas, Chile, Qinghai) as proof; (iii) chipmakers/policymakers should treat compute-at-the-resource as a chip-allocation and export-control question; (iv) standardize a transparent J/token disclosure so the epsilon uncertainty that dominates this analysis can be closed. Bookend the opening 'export the watt as a token' phrase. Bound the boldest vision with a horizon ('within this decade').

risksAndCounterarguments: Hardware depreciation, not electricity, dominates total cost (~60% chips vs ~4-7% energy in Epoch AI's TCO), so cheap power at the source improves margins only modestly and ~$2.3T / ~40M GPUs makes filling 60 GW a multi-decade, chip-supply-limited build-out, not a near-term switch — the claim is marginal-economic and directional, not a literal 'replace the transmission line tomorrow.'

Latency-sensitive and data-locality-bound workloads (interactive chat, real-time, data-resident enterprise/regulated inference) cannot relocate to a remote plateau; only the batchable fraction (training, batch and reasoning inference, synthetic-data generation, agentic background jobs) qualifies — though that fraction is large and growing (reasoning models exceeded 50% of usage by late 2025).

Why not just build the data center near demand and import cheap power, or near chips/talent? Near-demand siting forgoes both the stranded-power discount and avoided transmission, and competes for congested grids and interconnection queues — but it wins on latency, talent, supply chain, and avoids single-site geopolitical risk.

Firm, dispatchable hydro has high grid/system value (storage, flexibility, peaking) that is wasted if dedicated to constant-baseload compute; the opportunity cost is real wherever a grid can absorb the power — here largely notional because local demand is ~4% of output and 2025 curtailment is 30%+, but it would not hold at a well-connected site.

Water and cooling at high altitude, extreme seismicity (site on the Indus-Yarlung suture, M8.5 design, 2017 Ms6.9 triggered >1,820 landslides), thin air reducing air-cooling efficiency, and the logistics of hauling millions of GPUs into one of Earth's most inaccessible regions are serious physical risks the model must survive.

Jevons/rebound: making tokens cheaper by tapping near-free stranded energy may expand total AI demand and total energy and hardware use rather than reduce footprint — the framing monetizes waste but does not by itself bound aggregate consumption.

Geopolitics of compute: concentrating frontier compute at a single state-controlled site on a contested trans-boundary river (Brahmaputra, India/Bangladesh downstream) compounds export-control, data-sovereignty, single-point-of-failure, and water-security concerns; the same token-export logic is more benign at distributed stranded-renewable sites in Texas, Chile, Quebec, and the Nordics, which should be the generalizable case rather than this one flagship.

Chip export controls and supply concentration could make it impossible to legally or physically site the required accelerators at a given resource, decoupling the energy advantage from realizable compute and undermining the model precisely where stranded power is most abundant.
openQuestions: What is the true production-fleet energy-per-token (epsilon) for frontier and reasoning workloads, and how fast is it falling? This single parameter spans ~100x and dominates every headline number; standardized J/token disclosure is the highest-value missing data.
What share of global token demand is genuinely latency-insensitive and relocatable today, and how does that fraction evolve as agentic/reasoning/batch workloads grow relative to interactive chat?

At what delivered-power price and transmission distance does token export beat electron export on a full delivered-value-per-kWh basis, and where is the crossover for real sites (Tibet, Texas, Chile, Qinghai, Nordics)?

Can chip supply, capital, and construction logistics realistically deliver even a few GW of compute to a remote, seismically active, high-altitude site on the timescale of the dam's ~2033 commissioning, and what is the realistic ramp?

How should the grid/system value of firm hydro be priced against constant-baseload compute when local demand is negligible but could grow, and what hybrid (compute + selective electron export + storage) optimizes total value?

What governance, export-control, and trans-boundary-water frameworks are needed before concentrating frontier compute at a single state-controlled mega-site, and do distributed stranded-renewable sites avoid these risks while capturing most of the value?

Does monetizing stranded/curtailed energy as cheap tokens trigger net-positive substitution (displacing dirtier compute elsewhere) or net rebound (expanding total AI energy and hardware demand), and how would we measure the difference?

What is a defensible, regularly updated estimate of global annual token throughput (the denominator), given definitional inconsistency between API-only and all-surface multimodal counts and several-fold annual growth?
